mainTopic: Early death, and the פסוקים about strict Divine judgment that made רבי יוחנן cry
overview: This amud opens with the end of a story about רב ביבי בר אביי and the מלאך המות. The מלאך המות explains how he took a woman before her time, and he says that her lost years are given to a תלמיד חכם who lets go of insults. The גמרא then goes back to a list of frightening פסוקים that made רבי יוחנן cry. These include ה׳ being 'incited' against איוב and ה׳ not trusting even His holy ones, which a story about a fig picker helps explain. Next comes the פסוק in מלאכי, where ה׳ is both judge and witness. Other sages draw lessons from that same פסוק: light sins are weighed like severe ones, twisting a גר's case is like twisting ה׳'s, and true regret brings forgiveness right away. רבי יוחנן also cried over ה׳ judging 'every hidden thing, whether good or bad'. The גמרא gives examples such as disgusting someone without meaning to, or giving צדקה in a way that embarrasses the poor person or brings suspicion on a woman. Finally it explains 'evils and troubles' in two ways, and the amud ends with רב's teaching on הסתר פנים, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: How the messenger took the woman
steps.stepSummary: The מלאך המות's messenger finishes explaining how he was able to take the woman he brought by mistake: she burned herself, her luck dropped, and he took her.
steps.simpleTranslation: She was sweeping out the oven. She took the hot coals and put them on top of her foot. She got burned, her luck went down, and I brought her.
steps.whatsHappening: The מלאך המות's messenger finishes explaining how he was able to take a woman whose time had not come. She hurt herself, and that gave him an opening.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that a moment of danger or bad luck (מזל) can open the door for the מלאך המות to take someone early. This detail sets up רב ביבי's challenge in the next step: was he even allowed to do this?

keyTerms.meaning: And I brought her (took her life)

phrases.english: and she was sweeping out the oven,
she took [the coals] and put them on top of her foot,
she was burned and her luck was weakened,
and I brought her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story that began before this section, where the wrong Miriam was brought.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An injury that weakens a person's מזל gives the מלאך המות an opening to take that person early.

steps.title: Are you allowed to take someone early?
steps.stepSummary: רב ביבי בר אביי challenges the מלאך המות: do you have permission to take a person before their time?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ביבי בר אביי said to him: Do you have permission to act this way?
steps.whatsHappening: רב ביבי בר אביי challenges the מלאך המות. He asks whether it is allowed to take someone whose time has not come.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The assumption behind the question is that every person has a set lifespan. If so, taking someone early looks like overstepping that limit.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב בִּיבִי בַּר אַבָּיֵי:
phrases.english: Rav Beivai bar Abaye said to him:
phrases.notes: "Him" means the מלאך המות.

phrases.english: Do you have permission to act this way?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges what the מלאך המות just described doing.
steps.kashyaTarget: The מלאך המות taking the woman before her time
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If each person has a fixed lifespan, cutting it short seems to have no permission behind it.

steps.title: Some people are swept away without judgment
steps.stepSummary: The מלאך המות answers with a פסוק showing that some people die without a judgment against them.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Is it not written, "But there are those swept away without justice"?
steps.whatsHappening: The מלאך המות defends himself by quoting a פסוק from משלי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says some people are "swept away without judgment." That shows a person can die without a heavenly verdict against them, so taking someone early is allowed.

phrases.english: He said to him: And is it not written:
"But there are those swept away without justice"?
phrases.notes: משלי 13:23

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב ביבי's challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every death needs a judgment, so taking someone early is not allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק shows that some people die without a judgment.

steps.title: Each generation has a fixed time
steps.stepSummary: רב ביבי pushes back with a פסוק from קהלת suggesting each generation has a set lifespan.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: But isn't it written, "One generation goes and another generation comes"?
steps.whatsHappening: רב ביבי answers the מלאך המות's פסוק with a פסוק of his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "A generation goes and a generation comes" suggests each generation has a fixed, complete time. So how can one person be cut out early?

keyTerms.meaning: But is it not written? (opens a challenge from a פסוק)

phrases.english: He said to him: But isn't it written:
"One generation goes and another generation comes"!
phrases.notes: קהלת 1:4

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that people can be taken early
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק implies a generation's time is fixed, so no one should be taken before it is done.

steps.title: Held until the generation's time is complete
steps.stepSummary: The מלאך המות explains that he keeps those souls with him until their generation's time is up, and only then hands them to דומה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: I shepherd them until the generation's years are complete, and then I hand them over to דומה.
steps.whatsHappening: The מלאך המות reconciles the two פסוקים. The person dies early, but the soul stays in his care until its full time is up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both פסוקים are true. The body is taken early ("swept away"), but the soul's set time is still kept, because it is only passed to דומה, the angel in charge of the souls of the dead, when the generation's time ends.

keyTerms.meaning: The angel in charge of the souls of the dead

phrases.english: He said: I shepherd them
until the generation's [years] are complete,
and then I hand him over to Dumah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from קהלת.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Dying early cancels the generation's fixed time.
steps.terutzMaskana: The soul is held until the time is up, so the fixed time is still honored.

steps.title: What happens to the lost years?
steps.stepSummary: רב ביבי asks what happens to the years of life the person never got to live.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: In the end, what do you do with his years?
steps.whatsHappening: רב ביבי asks a follow-up question. What happens to the years this person lost?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the soul waits, the years of actual life in this world are still missing. רב ביבי wants to know whether those years are simply lost.

phrases.english: He said to him: In the end,
what do you do with his years?
phrases.notes: He means the extra years the person would have lived if he had not been taken early.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the answer in step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What becomes of the unlived years of someone taken early

steps.title: The years go to a forgiving Torah scholar
steps.stepSummary: The מלאך המות answers that the lost years are given to a צורבא מרבנן who lets go of insults, and he takes the dead person's place.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: If there is a young Torah scholar who overlooks wrongs done to him, I add those years to him, and he takes the place of the one who died.
steps.whatsHappening: The מלאך המות explains that the lost years are not wasted. They are added to a תלמיד חכם who lets go of insults against him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A צורבא מרבנן who is "מעביר על מדותיו", meaning he doesn't hold on to wrongs done to him, receives the extra years. That way the generation's total time stays complete.

keyTerms.meaning: Who lets go of matters done against him

steps.whatToRemember: A person taken early still has his time counted: his soul waits until his generation is done, and his unlived years go to a תלמיד חכם who forgives those who hurt him.
steps.whyThisMatters: This story shows how highly חז"ל value letting go of insults. It can even bring a person extra years of life.

phrases.english: He said: If there is a young Torah scholar
who lets go of his personal matters,
phrases.notes: He means someone who doesn't hold a grudge when people insult or wrong him.

phrases.english: I add them to him,
and he becomes his replacement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6 and closes the story.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The unlived years are added to a forgiving צורבא מרבנן, who takes the place of the dead person.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן cries: a servant whose master is incited
steps.stepSummary: Back to the earlier topic: רבי יוחנן cried over the פסוק in איוב where ה׳ says the שטן incited Him against איוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי יוחנן reached this verse, he cried: "You incited Me against him, to destroy him without cause." A servant whose master can be incited against him and is incited, is there any hope for him?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to its earlier list of פסוקים that made רבי יוחנן cry, and adds one from איוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ה׳ says the שטן "incited" Him against איוב. רבי יוחנן is shaken by this: if a master can be pushed by others to act against his servant, how can the servant protect himself?

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּי מָטֵי לְהַאי קְרָא, בָּכֵי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan, when he reached this verse, would cry:
"You incited Me against him, to destroy him without cause."
phrases.notes: איוב 2:3. ה׳ is speaking to the שטן about איוב.

phrases.english: A servant whose master others incite, and he is incited,
is there any remedy for him?!

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּי מָטֵי לְהַאי קְרָא בָּכֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story of the מלאך המות and returns to the series of פסוקים that made רבי יוחנן cry.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If ה׳ can be "incited" against a person, that person seems to have no protection, and this frightened רבי יוחנן.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן cries: He does not trust His holy ones
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן cried over another פסוק in איוב: if ה׳ does not trust even His holy ones, whom does He trust?
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי יוחנן reached this verse, he cried: "Behold, He puts no trust in His holy ones." If He does not trust His holy ones, whom will He trust?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another frightening פסוק that made רבי יוחנן cry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says ה׳ does not fully trust even His holy ones. רבי יוחנן reasons that if even they are not trusted, ordinary people have even more reason to fear.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן cried over פסוקים showing how strict Divine judgment is. Even איוב could be harmed because of incitement, and even the holy ones are not fully trusted.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּי מָטֵי לְהַאי קְרָא, בָּכֵי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan, when he reached this verse, would cry:
"Behold, He puts no trust in His holy ones,"
phrases.notes: איוב 15:15

phrases.english: if He does not trust His holy ones,
in whom will He trust?

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּי מָטֵי לְהַאי קְרָא בָּכֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another פסוק to רבי יוחנן's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If even the holy ones are not trusted, no one can feel secure before Divine judgment.

steps.title: The fig picker who took the unripe figs
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן sees a man picking unripe figs because they last longer on a trip, and he says this explains the פסוק 'הן בקדושיו לא יאמין'.
steps.simpleTranslation: One day רבי יוחנן was walking on the road. He saw a man picking figs. The man left the ripe ones and took the unripe ones. רבי יוחנן asked him: aren't the ripe ones much better? The man answered: I need these for the road. The unripe ones will stay good, and the ripe ones will not. רבי יוחנן said: this is what the פסוק means, 'Behold, He does not trust His holy ones.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story that shows what the פסוק from step 9 means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man picks figs early so they won't spoil on the way. In the same way, ה׳ sometimes takes a צדיק from the world early, because He knows the person might go bad later. This gives a new meaning to 'He does not trust His holy ones': ה׳ does not rely on them staying good forever.

keyTerms.meaning: They keep, they stay good and don't spoil
This is what is written; this matches the פסוק
Behold, He does not trust His holy ones (איוב)

steps.whyThisMatters: This story sets up an idea: not every early death is a punishment. That idea is exactly what the next step will challenge.

phrases.aramaic: יוֹמָא חַד הֲוָה קָא אָזֵיל בְּאוֹרְחָא,
phrases.english: One day he was walking along the road,
phrases.notes: 'He' is רבי יוחנן, who cried over the פסוק in step 9.

phrases.english: he saw a certain man
who was picking figs.
He left the ones that were ripe
and took the ones that were not ripe.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לָאו הָנֵי מְעַלָּן טְפֵי?
phrases.english: He said to him: Aren't these much better?
phrases.notes: He is pointing at the ripe figs.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָנֵי לְאוֹרְחָא בָּעֵינַן לְהוּ,
phrases.english: He said to him: I need these for the road;
these will last, and those will not last.
He said: This is what is written:
"Behold, He does not trust His holy ones."
phrases.notes: איוב 15:15

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹמָא חַד הֲוָה קָא אָזֵיל בְּאוֹרְחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a story that explains the פסוק רבי יוחנן cried over in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ה׳ sometimes takes righteous people early, before they can go bad, just as a traveler picks figs before they ripen so they will last.

steps.title: Challenge from the young student who died
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: רבי אלכסנדרי said a young student who died could have lived if he wanted. But according to the fig idea, maybe he was a צדיק taken early?
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really so? There was a student who lived near רבי אלכסנדרי and died young. רבי אלכסנדרי said: if this scholar had wanted, he would have lived. But if the fig idea is true, maybe he was one of those 'holy ones' ה׳ took early?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the fig-picker idea using a story about רבי אלכסנדרי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלכסנדרי blamed the student's early death on the student's own actions. But if צדיקים can be taken early just to protect them, how could he be sure? Maybe this student died for that good reason, not because he did something wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? A word the גמרא uses to begin a challenge
And if it is so (if the earlier idea is true)

phrases.english: Is that so?
But there was a certain student
who lived in the neighborhood of Rabbi Alexandri
and died while young,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַר: אִי בָּעֵי הַאי מֵרַבָּנַן, הֲוָה חָיֵי.
phrases.english: and he said: If this scholar had wanted, he would have lived.
phrases.notes: 'He said' is רבי אלכסנדרי. He means the student's own actions caused his early death.

phrases.english: And if it is so,
phrases.notes: If the fig-picker idea from step 10 is true.

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְמָא מֵ״הֵן בִּקְדוֹשָׁיו לֹא יַאֲמִין״ הֲוָה?
phrases.english: perhaps he was one of "Behold, He does not trust His holy ones"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the idea from step 10 by pointing to a case where an early death was blamed on the person.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that righteous people may be taken early to protect them.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If that idea is true, רבי אלכסנדרי could not confidently say the student died because of his own behavior; maybe he was a צדיק taken early.

steps.title: That student disrespected his teachers
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the student was disrespectful to his teachers, so רבי אלכסנדרי knew his death was a punishment.
steps.simpleTranslation: That student used to disrespect his teachers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge: this student was known to be disrespectful to his teachers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלכסנדרי was not guessing. He knew this student acted badly toward his teachers, so the student was not one of the 'holy ones' taken early. Both ideas can be true: some early deaths are protection, and some are punishment.
steps.whatToRemember: An early death can come for two different reasons: ה׳ taking a צדיק before he goes bad (the figs), or a punishment for real sins (the student who disrespected his teachers).

phrases.english: That one used to disrespect his teachers.
phrases.notes: Literally 'kick at' his teachers, meaning he treated them with disrespect.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the case: this student was known to be a sinner.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The student might have been a צדיק taken early, so רבי אלכסנדרי couldn't blame him.
steps.terutzMaskana: The student disrespected his teachers, so his early death was clearly a punishment; the fig idea still stands for real צדיקים.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן cries: ה׳ is both judge and witness
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן cries over a פסוק in מלאכי where ה׳ comes close to judge and is a quick witness. If the master is both judge and witness, what hope does the servant have?
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי יוחנן reached this פסוק, he cried: 'I will come near to you for judgment, and I will be a quick witness against the sorcerers, the adulterers, those who swear falsely, and those who hold back a worker's pay.' He said: a servant whose master brings him close to judge him, and hurries to testify against him, does he have any way out?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another פסוק that made רבי יוחנן cry, continuing the list from steps 8 and 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a judge and a witness are different people. Here ה׳ is both the judge and the witness, and He hurries to testify. So a person being judged has no way to escape, which is why רבי יוחנן cried.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who hold back a hired worker's pay
A fix, a way out, a remedy

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּי מָטֵי לְהַאי קְרָא, בָּכֵי:
phrases.english: When Rabbi Yochanan reached this verse, he cried:
"And I will come near to you for judgment,
phrases.notes: מלאכי 3:5

phrases.english: and I will be a quick witness against the sorcerers
and against the adulterers, and against those who swear falsely,
and against those who hold back a hired worker's pay."
A servant whose master brings him close to judge him,
and hurries to testify against him,
does he have any way out?!

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּי מָטֵי לְהַאי קְרָא, בָּכֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the list of פסוקים that made רבי יוחנן cry, after the side discussion about the figs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When ה׳ is both judge and quick witness, the one being judged has no way to escape.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן בן זכאי: small sins weighed like big ones
steps.stepSummary: On the same פסוק, רבי יוחנן בן זכאי says 'woe to us,' because the פסוק puts light sins next to severe ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן בן זכאי said: Woe to us, that the פסוק weighed light sins for us like severe ones.
steps.whatsHappening: A second sage reacts to the same פסוק from מלאכי, with a different scary point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק lists very severe sins, like sorcery and adultery, right next to holding back a worker's pay, which seems lighter. רבי יוחנן בן זכאי sees this as a warning: ה׳ treats the 'smaller' sins with the same seriousness as the big ones.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up רבי יוחנן (who cried in step 13) with רבי יוחנן בן זכאי here. They are two different sages from different times.
steps.whatToRemember: The פסוק in מלאכי scared the sages in two ways: ה׳ is both judge and witness (רבי יוחנן), and light sins are listed with severe ones (רבי יוחנן בן זכאי).

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai said:
Woe to us,
that the verse weighed for us
light sins like severe ones.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי: אוֹי לָנוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second reaction to the same פסוק from step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק treats light sins as seriously as severe ones, which is frightening for us.

steps.title: Twisting a convert's case is like twisting ה׳'s case
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש reads the word 'ומטי' in מלאכי as 'and turn Me aside,' so twisting a גר's judgment is like twisting ה׳'s.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: Anyone who twists the judgment of a convert is as if he twisted the judgment of the One above. It says 'and who turn aside the convert,' but the word is spelled so it can be read 'and turn Me aside.'
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש adds one more lesson from the same פסוק in מלאכי that the גמרא was just discussing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'ומטי גר,' those who turn aside a convert. ריש לקיש points out the spelling, which can be read 'ומטי' meaning 'and turn Me aside.' So hurting a גר's court case counts as an act against ה׳ Himself.

keyTerms.meaning: Of the One above, meaning ה׳
It is written (this is how the word is spelled)

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
Anyone who twists the judgment of a convert
is as if he twists the judgment of the One above,
as it says: "And who turn aside the convert"
phrases.notes: מלאכי 3:5, the same פסוק as the last two steps.

phrases.english: It is written "umatti" (and turn Me aside).
phrases.notes: The spelling lets you read it as 'turn Me aside,' as if the person is twisting ה׳'s own case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching drawn from the same פסוק in מלאכי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Twisting a convert's judgment is treated like twisting ה׳'s judgment, based on how 'ומטי' is spelled.

steps.title: Someone who regrets a sin is forgiven right away
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בר פפא learns from 'and do not fear Me' that people who do fear ה׳ and regret their sin are forgiven immediately.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא בר פפא said: Anyone who does something wrong and regrets it is forgiven right away. The פסוק says 'and do not fear Me,' which implies that if they do fear Me, they are forgiven right away.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא בר פפא takes the last words of the same פסוק and finds a comforting lesson in them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק lists sinners who are judged harshly because they 'do not fear Me.' רבי חנינא reasons the other way around: if the problem is not fearing ה׳, then someone who does fear Him and feels bad about the sin is forgiven at once. After the frightening teachings before this, this one offers hope.

keyTerms.meaning: Regrets, feels sorry for what he did

steps.whyThisMatters: It balances the harsh tone of the פסוק: real regret brings immediate forgiveness.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa said:
Anyone who does something (wrong) and regrets it
is forgiven immediately,
as it says: "And do not fear Me."
phrases.notes: These are the last words of the same פסוק, מלאכי 3:5.

phrases.english: This implies: if "they fear Me"
they are forgiven immediately.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching from the same פסוק, this time a hopeful one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who sins and regrets it out of fear of ה׳ is forgiven immediately.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן cries over being judged for hidden things
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן cries over the פסוק in קהלת that ה׳ judges 'every hidden thing,' because it seems even accidental sins are judged like deliberate ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי יוחנן reached this verse, he cried: 'For God will bring every deed into judgment, over every hidden thing.' A servant whose master weighs his accidental sins like his deliberate ones, what hope does he have?!
steps.whatsHappening: This is another פסוק that made רבי יוחנן cry, like the one in מלאכי earlier. He fears being judged even for things a person did not realize he did wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Hidden' things are sins the person himself was not aware of. If ה׳ judges those too, it looks like accidental sins are treated as seriously as deliberate ones. רבי יוחנן asks what hope a servant has under such a strict master.

keyTerms.meaning: A fix, hope, a way out

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּי מָטֵי לְהַאי קְרָא, בָּכֵי:
phrases.english: When Rabbi Yochanan reached this verse, he cried:
"For every deed, God
will bring into judgment, over every hidden thing."
phrases.notes: קהלת 12:14

phrases.english: A servant whose master weighs for him
accidental sins like deliberate ones,
does he have any hope?!

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּי מָטֵי לְהַאי קְרָא, בָּכֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another פסוק that made רבי יוחנן cry, in the same style as step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ה׳ judges even 'hidden' sins, which makes it seem accidental sins are weighed like deliberate ones.

steps.title: What counts as a 'hidden thing'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what kind of act the פסוק means by 'every hidden thing.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What is meant by 'over every hidden thing'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question to explain the פסוק רבי יוחנן cried over. This sets up the answers of רב and שמואל in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'hidden thing' is vague. The גמרא wants a concrete example of something a person does without realizing it is wrong, yet still gets judged for.

phrases.english: What is meant by "over every hidden thing"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the phrase in the פסוק from step 17.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A concrete example of a 'hidden' act that ה׳ judges.

steps.title: Disgusting someone without meaning to
steps.stepSummary: רב says it means killing a louse in front of someone who is disgusted by it; שמואל says it means spitting in front of someone who is disgusted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: This is someone who kills a louse in front of his friend, and the friend is disgusted by it. שמואל said: This is someone who spits in front of his friend, and the friend is disgusted.
steps.whatsHappening: רב and שמואל each give an example of a 'hidden thing.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both examples the person did not intend to bother anyone, so the harm is 'hidden' from him. Still, his friend was disgusted, and ה׳ judges him for causing that discomfort. רב and שמואל give similar ideas with different examples.

phrases.english: Rav said:
This is one who kills a louse in front of his friend
and (his friend) is disgusted by it.

phrases.aramaic: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: זֶה הָרָק בִּפְנֵי חֲבֵירוֹ וְנִמְאָס.
phrases.english: And Shmuel said: This is one who spits in front of his friend, and (the friend) is disgusted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A 'hidden thing' is causing someone disgust without meaning to, like killing a louse (רב) or spitting (שמואל) in front of him.

steps.title: How can a good deed be judged?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the end of the פסוק means: 'whether good or whether bad.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What is meant by 'whether good or whether bad'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about the end of the same פסוק in קהלת. This sets up the answer of the school of רבי ינאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק suggests ה׳ judges even 'good' acts. The גמרא wants to know how a good deed could bring judgment.

phrases.english: What is meant by "whether good or whether bad"?
phrases.notes: These are the closing words of the same פסוק, קהלת 12:14.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next phrase of the same פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How a 'good' act can be something ה׳ brings into judgment.

steps.title: Giving צדקה in public
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ינאי says this means giving צדקה to a poor person in public.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ינאי said: This is someone who gives צדקה to a poor person in public.
steps.whatsHappening: The school of רבי ינאי answers: the 'good' that is judged is giving צדקה in a public way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Giving צדקה is a good deed, which is why the פסוק calls it 'good.' But doing it in public embarrasses the poor person, so the giver is judged for that harm.

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yannai said:
This is one who gives charity to a poor person in public.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The 'good' that is judged is giving צדקה in public, which shames the poor person.

steps.title: רבי ינאי scolds a man who gave in public
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי saw a man give a coin to a poor person in public and told him it would have been better not to give at all than to embarrass him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like the story of רבי ינאי, who saw a man giving a זוז to a poor person in public. He said to him: It would have been better if you had not given him anything, than now, when you gave to him and embarrassed him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the answer with a story about רבי ינאי himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ינאי says that embarrassing the poor person was so harmful that giving nothing would have been better. This shows clearly why a public gift of צדקה can turn into something ה׳ judges.
steps.whatToRemember: ה׳ judges even small or 'good' acts if they hurt another person: causing disgust (רב and שמואל) or embarrassing a poor person with public צדקה (רבי ינאי).
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches a lasting lesson about giving צדקה: protect the poor person's dignity, or the מצוה itself can become a wrong.

phrases.english: Like this story of Rabbi Yannai,
who saw a certain man
giving a zuz to a poor person in public.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מוּטָב דְּלָא יְהַבְתְּ לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: He said to him: It would have been better had you not given him,
than now, that you gave him and embarrassed him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story that illustrates and supports the answer in step 21.
steps.raayaObject: That giving צדקה in public counts as a 'good' deed ה׳ still judges.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of רבי ינאי telling a man that giving nothing would have been better than embarrassing the poor person.

steps.title: Giving charity to a woman in private
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי שילא says 'whether good or whether bad' refers to giving צדקה to a woman in secret, because it puts her under suspicion.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי שילא say: This is someone who gives charity to a woman in private, because he causes people to suspect her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer to what 'whether good or whether bad' means. The school of רבי שילא offers a different example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Giving צדקה in secret is usually the best way to give. But when a man secretly gives to a woman, people may suspect something improper is going on between them. So a 'good' act turns 'bad' because of how it is done.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the גמרא is against giving צדקה in secret. Secret giving is normally ideal. The problem here is only the suspicion it creates in this one specific case.

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Sheila say:
This is one who gives charity to a woman in private,
since he brings her to suspicion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second explanation, different from the school of רבי ינאי's, of 'whether good or whether bad.'
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does 'whether good or whether bad' refer to?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Giving צדקה privately to a woman, which brings suspicion on her.

steps.title: Sending uncut meat to one's wife before Shabbat
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the פסוק refers to a man who sends his wife meat that has not been cut up and prepared on ערב שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: This is someone who sends his wife meat that is not cut up, on Friday afternoons before שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a third example of what 'whether good or whether bad' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sending food for שבת is a kind act. But meat still needs its forbidden parts removed, and on ערב שבת the wife is rushed. She may miss them and cook something forbidden, so the good act leads to a bad result.

keyTerms.meaning: Fridays before שבת, when everyone is rushing

phrases.english: Rava said:
This is one who sends his wife meat
that is not cut up, on Shabbat eves.
phrases.notes: 'Not cut up' means the forbidden parts, like the גיד הנשה, haven't been removed yet. A rushed wife might miss them.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר זֶה הַמְשַׁגֵּר לְאִשְׁתּוֹ בָּשָׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another alternative explanation of the same words of the פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does 'whether good or whether bad' refer to?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Sending unprepared meat to one's wife on ערב שבת, which risks her cooking forbidden parts in her rush.

steps.title: But רבא himself sent such meat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא: he himself used to send uncut meat to his wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבא himself used to send meat like this!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that רבא seems to do exactly what he just said is wrong. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If sending uncut meat on ערב שבת is a 'bad' act, how could רבא do it himself? The challenge is about his own behavior contradicting his teaching.

phrases.english: But Rava himself would send [such meat]!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's statement using his own conduct.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's teaching that sending uncut meat on ערב שבת is wrong
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא himself did this act, so either the act is fine or his conduct contradicts his teaching.

steps.title: רבא's wife was an expert
steps.stepSummary: רבא's wife, the daughter of רב חסדא, was different, because he knew she was an expert.
steps.simpleTranslation: The daughter of רב חסדא is different, because רבא was sure that she was an expert.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. רבא's case was special because of who his wife was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry was that a rushed wife would not notice the forbidden parts. רבא's wife was skilled enough to handle the meat correctly even in a rush, so there was no danger. The general rule stays the same, and her case is an exception.

keyTerms.meaning: Daughter of רב חסדא, who was רבא's wife

steps.whatToRemember: A worry about mistakes does not apply to someone known to be an expert. The rule against sending uncut meat still holds for most people.

phrases.english: The daughter of Rav Chisda is different,
phrases.notes: She was רבא's wife.

phrases.english: since he was sure about her that she was an expert.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge to רבא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the person involved is different
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא's own behavior contradicts his rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule applies to ordinary cases. רבא's wife was an expert, so the risk did not exist for her.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן cries over 'many evils and troubles'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן cried at the פסוק 'many evils and troubles will find him,' asking what hope a servant has when his master sends him troubles.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי יוחנן reached this פסוק, he cried: 'And it shall be, when many evils and troubles come upon him.' A servant whose master brings evils and troubles on him, does he have any way out?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to another פסוק that made רבי יוחנן cry. He feels that troubles sent by God leave a person with no escape.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The servant is the Jewish people, and the master is God. If God Himself sends the troubles, there seems to be no fix. The fear is about how serious punishment from Heaven is.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּי מָטֵי לְהַאי קְרָא, בָּכֵי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan, when he reached this verse, would cry:
"And it shall be, when there come upon him
many evils and troubles."
phrases.notes: דברים 31:21

phrases.aramaic: עֶבֶד שֶׁרַבּוֹ מַמְצִיא לוֹ רָעוֹת וְצָרוֹת,
phrases.english: A slave whose master brings upon him evils and troubles,
does he have any remedy?!

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כִּי מָטֵי לְהַאי קְרָא בָּכֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves away from the קהלת פסוק to a new פסוק that made רבי יוחנן cry.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Troubles sent by one's Master in Heaven leave a person with no easy escape.

steps.title: What are 'evils and troubles'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the פסוק uses two words, 'evils' and 'troubles.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'evils and troubles' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the meaning of the double phrase in the פסוק. This sets up רב's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says both 'evils' and 'troubles,' which sounds repetitive. The גמרא wants to know what extra idea the two words together are teaching.

phrases.english: What is "evils and troubles"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the words of the פסוק רבי יוחנן cried over.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of suffering is meant by the double phrase 'evils and troubles'?

steps.title: Troubles whose cures clash, like hornet and scorpion
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that these are evils that make each other worse, such as being stung by both a hornet and a scorpion.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: Evils that become troubles for each other, like a hornet and a scorpion.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question. 'Evils and troubles' means problems whose cures clash with each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each problem on its own could be treated. But when they come together, curing one makes the other worse, so there is no way to fix both. This explains why רבי יוחנן asked if there is any remedy.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב, 'evils and troubles' are problems that block each other's cures, which is why רבי יוחנן felt there was no remedy. שמואל gives a different explanation in the next step.

phrases.english: Rav said:
Evils that become troubles to one another,
such as a hornet and a scorpion.
phrases.notes: A hornet sting needs a cold treatment, and a scorpion sting needs a hot one. So you can't treat both at once.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב רָעוֹת שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוֹת צָרוֹת זוֹ לָזוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the double phrase.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Troubles whose cures work against each other, like a hornet sting and a scorpion sting at the same time.

steps.title: שמואל's example: the lender who rescues and then presses
steps.stepSummary: שמואל gives a second explanation of 'evils and troubles': someone who lends money to a poor person in his moment of need and then pressures him for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: This is someone who provides money to a poor person at the time of his pressure.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers the same question from step 28 ('why two words?') in a different way than רב did. His picture is a loan given at a hard moment that soon turns into a new burden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, the 'two troubles' were two pains that hit at once, like a hornet and a scorpion. For שמואל, the 'help' itself becomes the second trouble: the loan eases the first crunch, but then the lender demands repayment and the poor man is pressured all over again. So one trouble leads straight into the next.

keyTerms.meaning: at the time of his pressure, his moment of need

steps.confusionAlert: שמואל is not criticizing lending money to the poor. He is describing a case where the help comes with quick pressure to pay it back, so it turns into another trouble.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said:
This is one who provides money to the poor person
at the time of his pressure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the question in step 28, different from רב's answer in step 29.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the פסוק says both 'evils' and 'troubles.'
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A loan given to a poor person in hard times, which soon brings the new pressure of paying it back.

steps.title: רבא's folk saying that illustrates שמואל
steps.stepSummary: רבא connects שמואל's explanation to a popular saying: a poor man can't find a coin for food, but he finds one when a lender is hanging on him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: This is what people say: A זוז for produce is not found; for hanging it is found.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא brings a well-known saying that shows שמואל's idea in real life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A poor man can't scrape together money for basic food. But when a lender hangs onto him and won't let go, he somehow has to come up with it. That shows how the pressure of paying back is a fresh, painful trouble.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what people say (a popular saying)

phrases.english: Rava said:
This is what people say:
A zuz for produce is not found,
for hanging, it is found.
phrases.notes: 'Hanging' means a lender hanging onto him and pressing him. Then he is forced to find the money somehow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports and illustrates שמואל's explanation in step 30.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The popular saying shows that a lender's pressure is a real, crushing trouble for the poor, just as שמואל said.

steps.title: Anyone who never experiences God hiding His face is not 'from them'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a פסוק about God hiding His face from Israel. Then רב ברדלא בר טביומי, in the name of רב, says that anyone who never experiences this is not part of the people. He begins a second, similar statement.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Then My anger shall be kindled against them on that day, and I will forsake them, and I will hide My face from them.' רב ברדלא בר טביומי said that רב said: Anyone who is not under hiding of the face is not from them. Anyone who is not under 'and they shall be devoured'...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new פסוק on the same theme of troubles and gives רב's reading of it. The second half of the statement is only starting here and continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says God will hide His face 'from them,' meaning from the Jewish people. רב reads this the other way around too: going through הֶסְתֵּר פָּנִים is a sign that you belong to 'them.' So someone who never feels it at all is not 'from them.' He then starts a matching statement about the next words of the same פסוק, 'and they shall be devoured.'

keyTerms.meaning: hiding of the face (God seeming distant)
he is not from them (not part of the people)

steps.confusionAlert: רב is not saying troubles are good or that suffering makes someone Jewish. He is reading the word 'from them' in the פסוק: the people this פסוק talks about are the ones who go through הֶסְתֵּר פָּנִים.

phrases.english: "Then My anger shall be kindled against them on that day,
phrases.notes: דברים 31:17

phrases.english: and I will forsake them, and I will hide My face from them."

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב בַּרְדְּלָא בַּר טַבְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Bardela bar Tavyumei said that Rav said:
Anyone who is not under hiding of the face,
is not from them.
phrases.notes: 'From them' is the same word at the end of the פסוק: the people God hides His face from.

phrases.english: Anyone who is not under "and they shall be devoured"...
phrases.notes: These words come next in the same פסוק. The sentence keeps going on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב בַּרְדְּלָא בַּר טַבְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב: כׇּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּהֶסְתֵּר פָּנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the 'evils and troubles' פסוק to a related פסוק about God hiding His face, on the same theme of troubles coming upon Israel.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Going through הֶסְתֵּר פָּנִים marks a person as part of the people the פסוק describes. Whoever never goes through it is not 'from them.'
